Refiner
ree-FY-ner
noun (one who purifies metal; a title of God)
From the verb “refine,” through Old French refiner, to purify; rendering the Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt or refine metal, applied to God's purifying of His people.

Biblical Definition

A refiner is one who melts ore or metal in the fire to separate the precious from the dross, and Scripture takes up the image to teach how God purifies His people through affliction. Malachi foretells the coming of the LORD's messenger and asks, “Who may abide the day of his coming?… for he is like a refiner's fire”; and the LORD “shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver,” purging the sons of Levi as gold and silver that they may offer an offering in righteousness. Isaiah hears God say, “I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.” The refiner's craft yields a rich theology of suffering: the fire is not destruction but purification; the dross is the sin and self that must be burned away; the heat is measured by the refiner's skill and watched until he sees his own image in the molten silver. So Peter writes that the trial of faith, more precious than gold, is tried with fire that it may be found unto praise and honour at the appearing of Jesus Christ. The dictionary marks the refiner against two errors: the prosperity gospel, which denies that God brings His people through the furnace at all, promising only ease; and the despairing heart, which reads affliction as the wrath of a judge rather than the skill of a Father. The Refiner sits—He does not abandon the crucible—and He brings forth His people as gold.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who purifies metal in the fire; in Scripture a title of God, who sits as a refiner and purifier (Malachi 3:3), burning away the dross of His people through the furnace of affliction until His image appears.

REFINER, noun. [Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt or refine.] One who melts metal in the fire to separate the precious from the dross.

A title of the LORD, who shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Malachi 3:3).

He is like a refiner's fire and fullers' soap, purging the sons of Levi.

He refines His people not with silver but in the furnace of affliction (Isaiah 48:10).

The trial of faith, tried with fire, is found unto praise at the appearing of Christ (1 Peter 1:7).

Key Scripture

Mal 3:3 — "And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness."

Mal 3:2 — "But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:"

Isa 48:10 — "Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction."

1 Pe 1:7 — "That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:"

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel denies the furnace altogether, while the despairing heart misreads it as the wrath of a judge; both miss the Refiner who sits over the crucible as a Father.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel and the word-of-faith movement teach that the believer's portion is health, wealth, and ease, and that affliction is a sign of insufficient faith or hidden sin. The image of the Refiner overthrows this. God Himself says He chose His people in the furnace of affliction; the trial of faith, tried with fire, is the very means by which gold is proven. To promise a fireless faith is to promise what God has never promised and to leave the suffering saint to conclude he has failed when in truth he is being purified.

The opposite error is the despair that reads the furnace as the wrath of a judge bent on destruction. But the prophet does not say God burns His people up; He says God sits as a refiner and purifies them, watching the silver until His image appears, removing the dross, never the metal. The fire is measured by a Father's skill and love, ordered to a holy end—an offering in righteousness, a faith found unto praise. The dictionary recovers the Refiner: God does bring His people through the fire, and He never leaves the crucible until the work is done.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt, refine, or test metal in the fire; the refiner's craft of separating dross from silver becomes the figure of sanctifying affliction.

expand to see more

Tsaraph, Hebrew, to smelt, refine, or assay metal by fire.

Keseph, Hebrew, silver, the metal most often named in the refining image.

Kur, Hebrew, the smelting furnace, “the furnace of affliction” of Isaiah 48:10.

The Greek dokimion (1 Peter 1:7), the “trial” or proving of faith as gold is proved.

The dross (Hebrew sig) figures the sin and self the fire burns away.

Usage

"In the sickroom the pastor read Malachi and reminded the sufferer that the Refiner sits, and does not leave the crucible."

"He warned against the prosperity gospel, for God chose His people in the furnace of affliction, not apart from it."

"She learned to read her trial as the refiner's fire, ordered by a Father until His image appeared in her."
